notes.meaning: God told Moses to cut two new stone tablets just like the first ones he had smashed. God promised to write the very same Ten Commandments on them. This showed that God was willing to renew his covenant with Israel after their sin with the golden calf, even though Moses had to supply the stones this time.

Moses was told to prepare himself and climb Mount Sinai early the next morning. He was to stand before God at the top of the mountain to receive the law. Meeting God required careful preparation and a reverent heart.

God commanded that no person or animal come near the mountain while Moses was there. When the law was first given, the elders and Joshua had walked part of the way up, but now Moses had to go completely alone. This strict rule reminded the people of God's great holiness and the seriousness of restoring the broken covenant.

Moses obeyed right away by cutting out two stone slabs and climbing the mountain at dawn with the tablets in his hands. The stones were small and light enough for one man to carry up the steep mountain. Moses showed prompt obedience as he carried blank stones, trusting God to write on them.

The Lord came down in the pillar of cloud and stood with Moses on the mountain. God then openly proclaimed his personal name, Yahweh, declaring his presence to his servant. The cloud revealed God's real presence while gently veiling his full glory from human eyes.

God passed before Moses and announced his true character. He declared that he is full of mercy, rich in grace, slow to anger, and overflowing with faithful love and truth. Instead of destroying rebellious Israel, God revealed himself as a God of deep compassion.

God showed that his faithful love extends to thousands of generations, forgiving all kinds of wrongdoing when people repent. At the same time, he will not leave unrepentant sinners unpunished, and the painful results of sin continue down through families who turn from him. God's mercy is vast, yet it never sets aside his perfect justice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following the Latin Vulgate, older translations such as the Douay-Rheims render the middle phrase as 'no man of himself is innocent before thee.'

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teachers use this verse to argue that Christians can remain bound by inherited 'generational curses' from their ancestors until a special prayer breaks them.

notes.meaning: As soon as Moses heard God speak, he quickly bowed down to the ground and worshiped. Hearing of God's wonderful goodness filled him with deep awe and humble reverence. True knowledge of God moves the heart to immediate praise.

Moses prayed that the Lord would stay with the people and travel in their midst. Even though Israel was stubborn and rebellious, Moses asked God to forgive their sin and claim them as his own special possession. Moses used the people's weakness as the very reason they needed God's presence so desperately.

God answered Moses by renewing his covenant with Israel. He promised to perform miraculous deeds that had never been seen anywhere on earth to bring them into the Promised Land. Everyone around them would witness the awesome power of God working for his people.

God commanded the people to obey everything he was ordering them that day. In return, he promised to drive out the six pagan nations living in Canaan before them. Israel's victory would come from God's power, not their own military strength.

The Israelites were warned never to make treaties or peace agreements with the pagan nations in the land. Making friendly alliances would lead the people into a trap and cause them to adopt evil practices. Compromising with idolatry would bring spiritual ruin.

Israel was commanded to wipe out all pagan worship sites by tearing down altars, smashing sacred stone pillars, and cutting down Asherah poles. Asherah was a Canaanite fertility goddess whose worship involved carved wooden poles. God wanted every trace of false religion removed so his people would not be tempted.

The Israelites were forbidden to worship any other god because the Lord is a jealous God. This holy jealousy is not petty envy, but a pure and protective love, like a husband who expects complete faithfulness from his bride. God will not share his worship with any idol.

God warned the people not to make treaties with the local inhabitants or eat food offered to their idols. If they made peace, their children would marry pagan spouses who would drag them into worshiping false gods. Joining with idolaters would lead the nation into spiritual unfaithfulness.

God gave a direct command never to cast idols out of melted metal. This rule was a sharp reminder of the golden calf they had made so recently. The true God cannot be pictured or honored by any handmade statue.

The people were commanded to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days in the month of Abib, which is early spring. They were to eat bread made without yeast to remember their hasty escape from Egypt. Keeping this feast reminded them each year of God's mighty deliverance.

Every firstborn male among the people and their animals belonged to God. Unclean animals like donkeys had to be redeemed, or bought back, with a lamb, and human firstborn sons were also to be redeemed with an offering. Coming before God required bringing a gift of gratitude rather than appearing empty-handed.

God commanded the people to work six days and rest on the seventh day. This Sabbath rest had to be kept even during the busiest farming seasons, such as plowing and harvesting. Trusting God meant putting worship and rest ahead of everyday farm work.

Israel was told to observe the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost, when the wheat harvest began. They also had to celebrate the Feast of Ingathering in the fall at the close of the farming year. These festivals honored the Lord as the giver of all food and blessing.

All Israelite men were required to gather before the Lord three times a year for these major feasts. God made an amazing promise that while the men were away worshiping, no enemy nation would attack or even covet their unprotected land. God showed that he would guard the homes and families of those who put obedience first.

God instructed the people not to offer the blood of sacrifices with leavened bread and not to leave any Passover meat until morning. They were also to bring the finest firstfruits of their harvest to God's house and never boil a young goat in its mother's milk. These laws protected the purity of God's worship from corrupt pagan customs.

God told Moses to write down these covenant terms so the people would know how to live. This written record renewed the covenant between God, Moses, and the whole nation of Israel. Putting God's laws into writing ensured they would not be forgotten.

Moses stayed on the mountain with the Lord for forty days and forty nights without eating food or drinking water. During this miraculous fast, God wrote the Ten Commandments onto the two stone tablets. This miracle confirmed the divine authority of the law that Moses brought down to the people.

Moses came down Mount Sinai carrying the two stone tablets, completely unaware that the skin of his face was shining. His face glowed because he had been speaking directly with the Lord. Being in God's holy presence left a visible reflection of divine glory on his face.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Jerome's Latin Vulgate translated the Hebrew word for shining as 'horned,' leading older translations like the Douay-Rheims to say Moses' face was horned, which influenced traditional religious art.

notes.meaning: When Aaron and the leaders saw Moses' face glowing with bright light, they were terrified to go near him. Their guilty consciences from making the golden calf made God's holy glory seem frightening. The visible brightness reminded them of God's pure holiness and their own sin.

Moses called out to the leaders, and Aaron and the rulers gathered the courage to return and speak with him. Afterward, all the people came near, and Moses taught them every command the Lord had spoken on the mountain. The radiant glory on his face proved that his message came straight from God.

When Moses finished delivering God's words to the people, he covered his face with a veil. He veiled himself so the bright glow would not continue to terrify the people during everyday conversations. This veil also pointed to the hidden and shadowy nature of the Old Testament laws compared to the gospel.

Whenever Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the Lord, he took the veil off. When he came out to tell Israel what God had commanded, his face would shine again, and then he would put the veil back on until his next meeting with God. Approaching God requires an uncovered face, and regular fellowship with him renews true spiritual radiance.
